surf.scene: Choose a well-spaced menu of model trade-offs.
story: The decision

A summarization system can reward both a useful summary and a faithful one. A weighted loss selects one compromise. A well-spaced collection of models gives users a range of quality–faithfulness balances to choose from.
The bottleneck

An equal change in the scalarization weight can move the solution a long distance in one region and barely move it in another. Uniform preferences can therefore spend several training slots on similar models while leaving other trade-offs sparsely represented.
The idea

Measure distance in objective space. SURF estimates how much of the front has been traversed at each weight, inverts that cumulative-distance map, and places training slots at equal distance targets. The scalarized inner solver can remain PPO, Adam, or another suitable solver.
findings: Choose weights by distance between solutions, so the available model slots cover the trade-offs more evenly.
Mean variation in the gaps between six models falls versus uniform weights. Lower means more even coverage of quality and faithfulness. Table 2.
Mean hypervolume, a measure of solution quality across both goals, rises in the same comparison. Higher is better. Table 2.
figure_read: From a weight to an objective vector
A weight produces a solved model and an objective vector. The cumulative arc-length map connects that vector back to the weight.
Known and reconstructed distance maps
Rule 1 inverts a known map. Rule 2 reconstructs it from solved points and refines it over outer iterations.
Reassign weights and resume training
Weights are reassigned and models warm-start from their previous slot. Each slot continues training with its chosen inner optimizer.

application: For summarization, the output is a set of differently aligned adapters. A user can select a quality–faithfulness balance without repeatedly encountering nearly identical trade-offs. Arc length depends on objective units, so the metric and normalization are part of the design choice.
cards: Match a distribution on the front

Traversal speed determines the density correction along a well-defined, monotone scalarization-induced path. Inverting its normalized arc-length map assigns weights to evenly spaced points on that path.
Refinement contracts to a resolution floor

Under Assumptions 1–3, sufficiently many segments, and the stated inner-solver budget, the combined CDF and optimization error contracts geometrically to O(N⁻²). Here N counts segments and the endpoints give N + 1 solutions.
faq: What determines uniform spacing?
Uniform spacing means equal arc-length gaps in the selected objective-space metric. The objective units and normalization determine that metric.
What does the interactive example demonstrate?

The quadratic gear toy in Appendix F.1 keeps the evaluation front fixed while changing traversal speed. The demo evaluates the exact scalarized solution and obtains arc-length targets by numerical integration and direct inversion.

retailagent.scene: A rising stock can hide a poorly timed policy.
story: The decision

At each interval, a frozen LLM sees an anonymized price history and chooses long or flat before the next return is revealed. The experiment can also show charts, account state, or the agent’s earlier self-authored memories.
The bottleneck

A policy can benefit from a rising stock while being flat during its strongest intervals. Measuring average exposure and alignment with the next return separately reveals when the policy allocated its exposure.
The idea

Subtract the return of constant exposure on the same stock-day. Audit the remaining timing term, shuffle saved actions to disrupt sequence alignment, and inspect how memory changes the policy’s persistence.
findings: Qwen3.5 text, per stock-day. One basis point is 0.01%. Negative timing means the chosen holding intervals were less favorable after matching average exposure. Table 1.
Shuffling actions within each day preserves time invested while weakening adverse timing. The ordering of the decisions matters. Table 1.
Adding one earlier memory reduces mean position changes per stock-day in the later-period experiment, compared with current memory alone. Table 3.
figure_read: Observation comes first
Text, chart, and multimodal pathways supply condition-specific history before the next action. Stock identity, date, news, and fundamentals are concealed in the principal numerical protocol.
State is generated by the policy
Position, ledger, account summary, and narrative memories depend on earlier decisions. They make the next prompt partly a consequence of the agent’s own behavior.
The optional learned channel
The soft-token encoder has a training stage. The standard and narrative conditions use a frozen LLM for inference, with observations and carried state specified by each condition.

panels.label: Shuffle controls
panels.title: Break the sequence, preserve exposure
panels.caption: Table 1 · Qwen3.5 text · 10-minute intervals
panels.reading: The negative timing is much larger in the intact trajectory. Same-day shuffling preserves the day’s action count while disrupting its alignment with subsequent intervals.
panels.protocol: Research-return labels are subsequent non-overlapping returns on historical equity paths. Timing is averaged in basis points per stock-day; percentile confidence intervals resample dates. The saved shuffle archive has a slightly different reported stock-day count from the intact row.

panels.label: Memory conditions
panels.title: One earlier memory and a more persistent policy
panels.caption: Table 3 · consistency directive · main-period conditional timing
panels.reading: The one-earlier-memory condition has the most negative timing of these four. In the later-period panel, it also makes fewer position changes: 1.7 per stock-day versus 2.5 for current memory only. Timing varies non-monotonically with memory-window length.
panels.protocol: Each main-period arm attempts 1,500 stock-days across 150 dates. Scored N excludes failed intervals and constant-action trajectories, so the timing estimates condition on both actions appearing. Position-change counts come from the separate later-period panel.

application: Exposure-matched timing diagnoses the agent’s interval choices on historical price paths. The study measures cross-sectional stock selection separately through IC and uses saved-action shuffles to examine sequential alignment.
cards: The action-weighted return decomposes exactly into average exposure times the day’s return plus centered timing. Always-long and always-flat policies score zero timing; complementing every action negates the timing score.

Modalities, model families, and state conditions are evaluated in their recorded sampling frames. The panel definitions and stock-day counts specify which action traces contribute to each timing estimate.
faq: What does inverting a schedule reveal?

On a fixed research-return path, complementing every long-or-flat action negates centered timing while preserving the same sequence of returns. This gives a sign diagnostic for the saved action trace.
How is the memory window counted?
The two-pass protocol creates a current-step memory. The window w counts earlier memories, so w = 0 provides the current memory and w = 1 adds one earlier memory.

birq.scene: Let a speech model improve its own training targets.
story: The decision

A self-supervised speech model learns by predicting pseudo-labels at masked frames. BEST-RQ obtains those labels from a fixed random projection of the unmasked audio features, avoiding an external pretrained label model.
The bottleneck

Raw-input labels stay fixed as the encoder learns. Intermediate-feature labels evolve with the same encoder that predicts them. Training must coordinate the changing targets with a stable reference task.
The idea

Keep both branches. BiRQ builds enhanced targets from unmasked intermediate features and preserves raw-input anchor targets. A differentiable Gumbel-softmax target and a penalty formulation connect label construction to the same training loop.
findings: Evolving model features supply enhanced targets. Raw audio features supply anchors. Both supervise prediction of masked speech frames.
Word error rate on the difficult test-other set, BEST-RQ versus BiRQ. The matched 155M models use 100 hours of labeled fine-tuning. Lower is better. Table 2.
Word error rate on AMI’s single distant microphone, BEST-RQ versus BiRQ. These 275M models are pretrained on YODAS. Lower is better. Table 3.
figure_read: Two views of the same utterance
The unmasked input supplies both target branches. The masked sequence goes through the prediction encoder; the loss is evaluated at masked positions.
Anchor and enhanced labels
The raw-input branch uses a fixed quantizer for anchor labels. The intermediate-feature branch applies random-projection quantization to the model’s evolving features.
Gradients through target construction
Gumbel-softmax makes enhanced target selection differentiable. The target and prediction share encoder parameters, so the update includes gradients through both paths.

panels.title: A different architecture and corpus
panels.caption: Table 3 · C3 · word error rate (%) ↓

panels.protocol: 10-layer 275M Conformer. Pretraining uses 100 SSL epochs on 5k hours of YODAS, followed by fine-tuning on 150h labeled AMI. IHM uses individual headset microphones and SDM uses a single distant microphone. Table 3 reports point estimates.

application: The enhanced-label objective learns from intermediate features while the anchor objective preserves the reference task. Because the anchor optimum is constant with respect to the model parameters, Algorithm 1 updates a weighted sum of the two loss gradients in one training loop.
cards: Enhanced learning with an anchor constraint
Minimize enhanced-label cross-entropy while keeping anchor-label loss within a prescribed gap of its optimum. Both objectives use the same encoder parameters and masked-frame prediction task.

Algorithm 1 combines enhanced-label and anchoring-loss gradients. The experiments use weights 0.1 and 2.4 with Gumbel-softmax temperature 0.5. Lemma 1 gives the penalty interpretation under its stated error-bound condition.
faq: Why keep the raw-input labels?
Raw-input labels provide a fixed reference task while the enhanced labels evolve with the encoder. Both target sources contribute to the shared training update.
How is the target-generating layer selected?
A pilot study motivates selecting a layer near 70% of encoder depth. The paper then evaluates layer and codebook choices through ablations, with training budgets specified for each comparison.

efficient-penalty.scene: Separate the sources of cost in a penalty method.
story: The decision

A bilevel learner chooses an outer variable while its inner variable solves another objective. A penalty makes inner suboptimality costly, but the chosen formulation and the update schedule determine which computation is actually required.
The bottleneck

There are three distinct costs: a penalty-scaled step-size restriction, two lower-level response estimates, and the extra structure of constraints that move with the outer decision. Treating them as one difficulty obscures which improvement applies.
The idea

Analyze the reduced objective to capture curvature cancellation, then alternate lower responses and outer updates. Upper-level flatness controls the bias from removing a value-function correction. The coupled extension incorporates constraint multipliers and boundary regularity.
findings: Under the analyzed regularity conditions, the curvature bound after lower-level optimization stays bounded as the penalty grows.
The PBGD-Free variant tracks the lower variable once, then updates the upper variable. Flatness controls the bias from the removed correction.
Mean runtime for PBGD-Free versus PBGD-BLOCC on diabetes classification. Mean test accuracy is 77.0% versus 77.6% across 20 splits. Table 7.
figure_read: The surface is a joint gradient
Changing x at an arbitrary fixed y can amplify the penalty contribution. That is the geometry seen by a generic joint update.
The line follows the inner response
The reduced gradient first accounts for lower-level optimization. The paper’s example shows far less variation along this response as the penalty increases.
Curvature along the optimized response
The example shows how following the optimized lower response changes the gradient’s dependence on the penalty. The reduced-smoothness theorems formalize that mechanism for their constraint regimes.

panels.label: Algorithm map
panels.title: Which cost does each update remove?
panels.caption: Sections 3–5 · analytical distinctions
panels.reading: Reduced smoothness and value-function removal are separate gains. The fixed-set PBGD-Free analysis covers a fully single-loop update; the coupled extension removes one response computation and still pays for the remaining constrained solve.
panels.protocol: Theorem 3.1 treats fixed-set reduced smoothness; Theorem 5.1 treats coupled smoothness under Assumptions 1–5, including strict complementarity and boundary regularity. Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 analyze the corresponding PBGD-Free variants under flatness.

panels.label: Constrained SVM
panels.title: Accuracy and runtime measure different outcomes
panels.caption: Table 7 · diabetes · mean ± standard deviation
panels.reading: PBGD-BLOCC has the highest mean accuracy and PBGD-Free the lowest mean runtime in this experiment. Their accuracy means are close relative to the standard deviations across splits.
panels.protocol: 20 random train–validation–test splits. Runtime ends at a validation-loss change below 10⁻⁵ or 50 epochs. PBGD-Free uses penalty 20 and the coupled method’s retained inner solve.

application: In LLM adaptation, flatness supports preference learning in a backbone with a supervised head. In constrained SVMs, outer violation bounds reshape the inner feasible set. The fixed-set and coupled algorithms address these different response structures.
cards: The scaled difference of nearby value functions admits a penalty-independent smoothness order under the theorem-specific regularity. Directional derivatives are analytical tools; the implementation still uses first-order information.

The flatness residual controls the stationarity neighborhood in both results. The fixed-set theorem uses the reduced objective. The coupled theorem measures stationarity of its multiplier-dependent surrogate and retains an inner solve.
faq: How does this relate to the conference papers?

It is a broader preprint developing the smoothness analysis and flatness-based updates together. The EUSIPCO page focuses on reduced curvature; the NeurIPS 2025 page focuses on value-function removal under flatness.
What role does flatness play in removing the correction?

Flatness controls upper-objective sensitivity near a lower-level optimum and bounds the bias from omission. The paper’s counterexample motivates this condition by showing a persistent error with the simplified outer partial gradient.

pbgd-free.scene: Learn a preference backbone while a head adapts.
story: The decision

In the paper’s LLM application, x contains LoRA parameters in the backbone and y is the output head. The head learns supervised fine-tuning (SFT); the backbone is guided by direct preference optimization (DPO) through that adapted head.
The bottleneck

A full penalty gradient estimates both the original SFT-optimal head and a perturbed head. Dropping the value-function correction saves one response estimate, but the removed term is multiplied by the penalty and can remain important.
The idea

Upper-level flatness bounds how the DPO objective varies around an SFT-optimal head. Together with the lower-level regularity conditions, it controls the stationarity error of one lower update followed by one outer update.
findings: Each iteration updates the lower variable once and then the upper variable, removing the extra solve used to track the lower-level minimum value.
A bound on how much the outer loss changes near a lower optimum controls the bias from skipping the value-function correction. Definition 1.
With the same training-time budget, Llama-3-3B preference loss is 0.7837 versus 0.8055 for ALRIGHT. Supervised loss is 0.8516 versus 0.8656. Lower is better. Table 2.
figure_read: Original and perturbed responses
Value-function-based methods track an original lower-level response alongside a perturbed response. Those are different optimization tasks.
The response retained by PBGD-Free
PBGD-Free keeps the perturbed lower-level tracking update and uses the upper partial gradient. It removes the response needed solely for the value-function correction.
Flatness bounds the omitted correction
The flatness inequality bounds upper-loss variation around the original lower-level response. Theorem 3 uses that condition to quantify the bias and residual introduced by the simplified update.

panels.title: Both preference and supervised losses
panels.caption: Table 2 · outcome (xT, yT) · losses ↓
panels.reading: PBGD-Free has the lowest reported loss in both columns for this fixed-time comparison. ALRIGHT is a bi-objective baseline, so its formulation differs from the bilevel methods.
panels.protocol: LoRA adaptation of the model labeled Llama-3-3b in the paper. DPO uses Dahoas/rm-hh-rlhf and SFT uses OpenOrca. Methods share a fixed training-time budget. Table 2 reports point estimates, with each method completing its own number of updates.

panels.title: Keep the backbone, fine-tune a new head
panels.caption: Table 2 · post-SFT outcome (xT, ỹ) · losses ↓
panels.reading: The PBGD-Free backbone also gives the lowest reported losses after head adaptation in this experiment. The SFT column here is a training loss, whereas the first panel reports an evaluated SFT loss.
panels.protocol: Phase S2 holds the learned backbone fixed and adapts the head on another SFT dataset under a fixed-time budget. Table 2 reports the resulting DPO and SFT losses. The paper evaluates generated output separately with BLEU.

application: The application separates preference learning in the backbone from supervised adaptation in the head. The second evaluation phase asks whether the learned backbone remains useful when only the head is trained for a new task. This is why the paper reports both the original outcome and post-SFT behavior.
cards: Omission can leave a persistent bias
Under generic Lipschitz conditions, Proposition 2 identifies a non-vanishing stationarity residual after omitting the correction. This motivates the flatness condition used to control the bias.

Under Assumption 2, uniform exponent 1 < α ≤ 1.5, the stated penalty and step sizes, and an averaged trajectory flatness residual δ, the theorem bounds average squared penalty-gradient norm by a decaying iteration term plus a flatness-dependent floor, as displayed above. Lemma 3 separately relates penalty stationarity to the original problem under its accuracy conditions.
faq: What does flatness measure?

Definition 1 measures upper-loss variation around a lower-level optimum using a distance exponent and a residual. The residual allows local variation, and the theorem carries its contribution into the stationarity bound.
How does the method extend to constraints?

This paper analyzes the unconstrained setting. The broader efficient-penalty preprint develops fixed-set and coupled-constraint extensions. The coupled method retains an inner solve for its constrained response.

smoothness.scene: Reduced curvature supports larger outer steps.
story: The decision

In bilevel optimization, penalty methods make a lower-level optimality gap expensive. A generic joint smoothness bound grows with the penalty, suggesting smaller gradient steps as the approximation is tightened.
The bottleneck

The outer algorithm follows a reduced objective after lower-level optimization. Bounding arbitrary joint directions can miss cancellation between the perturbed and original value functions. Constraints also invalidate the unconstrained shortcut that the inner gradient is zero.
The idea

Analyze their second-order directional derivatives together. For a fixed feasible set, the response direction is orthogonal to the lower gradient; for coupled constraints, multipliers account for the moving boundary. The resulting smoothness bound changes the outer iteration analysis.
findings: After lower-level optimization, increasing the penalty does not force the outer step-size order to shrink. Try the fixed-scale quadratic example.
The outer count improves from O(ε⁻¹·⁵) to O(ε⁻¹). Here ε is the squared gradient-norm tolerance; smaller means a stricter stopping target. Section III-B.
Constraints linear in the lower variable allow faster inner solves and retain the sharper total-work rate. General nonlinear constraints require more inner work.
figure_read: Fixed, coupled, and affine constraints
Fixed domains, general coupled constraints, and affine constraints use different inner solvers and have different total costs.
Smoothness and total complexity
O(1) smoothness supports a penalty-independent outer step-size order. The complexity column also counts the work of the selected inner solver.
The stationarity criterion
The tolerance ε applies to the squared generalized-gradient norm. The complexity exponents describe the work needed to meet that stationarity criterion.

panels.label: Fixed constraints
panels.title: A sharper analysis of alternating updates
panels.caption: Section III-B · outer and total complexity
panels.reading: The reduced analysis permits a constant step-size order. With projected gradient descent as the linearly convergent inner solver, logarithmic response-solve work gives the reported overall rate.
panels.protocol: Fixed nonempty closed convex feasible set; strong convexity of the lower objective, the stated Lipschitz and Hessian regularity, and constraint qualification. Proposition 2 uses ‖Gη(x)‖² < ε; Õ suppresses logarithmic factors.

panels.label: Coupled constraints
panels.title: The same outer rate can hide different total work
panels.caption: Section IV · improved BLOCC analysis
panels.reading: The general coupled regime requires more expensive primal-dual inner work. The affine special case permits a faster solver and retains the improved overall order.
panels.protocol: Theorem 3 adds a smooth domain boundary and twice-differentiable constraints with Lipschitz Hessians to Assumptions 1–4. Proposition 4 and Remark 1 separate the outer count from accelerated MaxMin solver cost. The original comparison is Table I.

application: For constrained bilevel optimization, choosing a step from the reduced geometry can avoid a penalty-scaled restriction inherited from a joint bound. The practical consequence depends on whether the lower response and its multipliers can be computed efficiently.
cards: The nearby value functions differ at a scale controlled by the penalty perturbation. Their directional curvature difference cancels the prefactor in Fγ under the stated assumptions.
The extension adds constraint and boundary regularity. The sharper bound supports the same outer iteration order, while the solver-dependent total complexity remains different across regimes.
faq: Which objective gets the sharper smoothness bound?
The O(1) bound describes the reduced objective along the optimized lower response. The joint penalty objective includes additional directions that move away from that response.
Where do second-order derivatives enter?
Second-order directional derivatives establish the smoothness bound. The algorithm evaluates first-order gradients using approximate lower responses and, for coupled constraints, their multipliers.

blocc.scene: Design a network while passengers choose their routes.
story: The decision

A network operator chooses infrastructure; passengers respond within the resulting network. In a constrained SVM, outer hyperparameters set violation limits and the inner model learns within those limits. Both are bilevel problems with a feasible set that changes with x.
The bottleneck

The lower-level value changes through the objective and through active constraints. An objective-only gradient can point in the wrong direction. A joint projection onto the full coupled feasible set can also become costly at large dimensions.
The idea

Use primal-dual responses to estimate the moving-boundary contribution. BLOCC combines them with a penalty reformulation and first-order updates, avoiding the full joint projection used by a direct constrained formulation.
findings: The update includes both changes in the lower objective and the influence of active constraints. Their multipliers supply the boundary contribution.
Mean diabetes test accuracy for BLOCC versus LV-HBA across 50 random train–validation–test splits. The reported variability is shown in the evidence table. Table 2.
On diabetes, BLOCC’s mean runtime is about 40% lower than LV-HBA’s at the reported stopping rule, with similar mean test accuracy. Table 2.
figure_read: The active constraint
Figure 1 uses g(x, y) = (y − 2x)² and the active bound y ≥ 3x. For x > 0, the constrained response is y_g^*(x) = 3x and the value is v(x) = x².
The sign error is concrete
The partial objective derivative gives −4x, while the derivative of the value is 2x. The multiplier-weighted constraint derivative restores the missing 6x.
The same example in the interactive plot
Changing x moves the feasible region. The interactive plot shows the resulting response, multiplier, and value-gradient decomposition for this example.

application: A larger test of coupled decisions

Transportation experiments use 3- and 9-node synthetic networks and a 26-node Seville network with 49,216 variables and 13,336 constraints. Table 3 lists runtime and operator utility. A missing baseline entry marks the 24-hour time limit.
cards: The constraint derivative belongs in the value gradient

Under Assumptions 1–4 and bounded multipliers, the derivative includes the partial objective term and the multiplier-weighted partial constraint derivative. Convexity is required in y; the outer problem can remain nonconvex.
Approximation, outer convergence, and inner cost

The penalty reformulation approximates lower-level optimality with controlled squared-distance error. The original analysis gives Õ(ε⁻²·⁵) overall work for general constraints and Õ(ε⁻¹·⁵) for its affine-in-y special case. The later EUSIPCO paper sharpens this analysis.
faq: Which projections does BLOCC use?

The primal-dual formulation handles the coupled inequalities through multipliers. Updates retain simple projections onto the separate variable domains and avoid a joint projection onto the coupled feasible set.
What convergence criterion does the analysis use?

The analysis uses a squared generalized-gradient stationarity criterion for the penalty reformulation. Strong inner convexity controls the lower-level response while the reduced outer objective can remain nonconvex.
